DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 23SMCV04144    Hearing Date: September 24, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

HARSHAL TOPIWALA,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

FEREIDOUN KHALILIAN, et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  23SMCV04144 

  Hearing Date:  September 24, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  Defendant's MOTION TO VACATE  

  entry of DEFAULT and default  

  judgment 

 

 

  

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is an action to recover damages arising from Plaintiff Harshil Topiwala’s investment of $585,500 in Defendant BlockChain Consulting Group, LLC (the “Company”). The Company is in the business of developing blockchain technology for use in the American Indian casino and gaming industry.  

Defendant Fred Khalilian executed a personal guaranty of Plaintiff’s investment in the Company. Khalilian guaranteed the repayment of Plaintiff’s capital investment within sixty (60) days of Plaintiff’s demand in the event Plaintiff did not see a return. Plaintiff did not see a return on his capital investment.  

On July 21, 2023, Plaintiff demanded payment on the guaranty.  Khalilian refused to pay. This action ensued.  

On September 1, 2023, Plaintiff filed a Complaint against Defendants. The Complaint alleges five claims for (1) breach of written contract, (2) declaratory relief, (3) intentional misrepresentation, (4) fraudulent inducement, and (5) unjust enrichment. The Complaint seeks actual damages in excess of $583,000, plus interest and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs. 

Plaintiff filed a proof of service showing Khalilian was served personally on October 20, 2023, and BlockChain Consulting Group LLC was served personally on December 26, 2023. Defendants did not respond within 30 days. Plaintiff successfully requested the entry of Defendants’ default, which was entered by the Clerk’s Office on February 26, 2024.  Plaintiff then requested default judgment on March 18, 2024, which this Court granted on June 14, 2024.  The judgment was against Defendants and in favor of Plaintiff in the amount of $622,026.98. 

This hearing is on Khalilian’s motion to vacate entry of default and default judgment.  Khalilian argues that he was in prison at the time service was made, and although he cannot dispute that the sheriff’s deputy in fact handed him the summons and complaint, he says he does not recall ever receiving it.  He also argues that the request for default/default judgment was mailed to his home when Plaintiff knew he was incarcerated.  In the alternative, Khalilian argues that the Court should allow “focused briefing and evidence” on the “correct principal, contractual maturity date, applicable interest rate, interest period, and resulting amount.” 

Khalilan had previously filed a motion to vacate default judgment which this Court denied without prejudice.  The prior motion was procedurally defective.  Khalilan has now corrected the deficiencies. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

Section 473(d) 

Code Civ. Proc. § 473(d) provides that “[t]he court may, upon motion of the injured party, or its own motion, correct clerical mistakes in its judgment or orders as entered, so as to conform to the judgment or order directed, and may, on motion of either party after notice to the other party, set aside any void judgment or order.”  

A defendant may move to set aside a default and default judgment based on improper service and lack of personal jurisdiction under Code Civ. Proc. §473(d). (Strathvale Holdings v. E.B.H. (2005) 126 Cal.App.4th 1241, 1250.) A “default judgment entered against a defendant who was not served with a summons in the manner prescribed by statute is void. Under § 473(d), the court may set aside a default judgment which is valid on its face, but void, as a matter of law, due to improper service.” (Ellard v. Conway (2001) 94 Cal.App.4th 540, 544.)  

Where service is challenged, the burden is on the plaintiff to prove the facts requisite to an effective service. (Lebel v. Mai (2012) 210 Cal.App.4th 1154, 1160.) 

Section 473.5 

Code Civ. Proc. § 473.5(a) provides: “When service of a summons has not resulted in actual notice to a party in time to defend the action and a default or default judgment has been entered against him or her in the action, he or she may serve and file a notice of motion to set aside the default or default judgment and for leave to defend the action. The notice of motion shall be served and filed within a reasonable time, but in no event exceeding the earlier of: (i) two years after entry of a default judgment against him or her; or (ii) 180 days after service on him or her of a written notice that the default or default judgment has been entered.” 

A notice of motion to set aside a default under section 473.5 “shall be accompanied by an affidavit showing under oath that the party’s lack of actual notice in time to defend the action was not caused by his or her avoidance of service or inexcusable neglect.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 473.5(b).)   

“’[A]ctual notice’ in section 473.5 ‘means genuine knowledge of the party litigant....’ [Citations.]  ‘[A]ctual knowledge’ has been strictly construed, with the aim of implementing the policy of liberally granting relief so that cases may be resolved on their merits.’ [Citation.]” (Ellard v. Conway (2001) 94 Cal.App.4th 540, 547.) 

“It is the policy of the law to favor, wherever possible, a hearing on the merits, and appellate courts are much more disposed to affirm an order where the result is to compel a trial upon the merits than they are when the judgment by default is allowed to stand and it appears that a substantial defense could be made. Stated another way, the policy of the law is to have every litigated case tried upon its merits, and it looks with disfavor upon a party, who, regardless of the merits of the case, attempts to take advantage of the mistake, surprise, inadvertence, or neglect of his adversary.” (Weitz v. Yankosky (1966) 63 Cal.2d 849, 854-855.) 

DISCUSSION 

Default judgment was entered on June 14, 2024.  Khalilian filed his motion to vacate more than two years after default judgment was entered.  Notwithstanding, there is no time-limit to filing a motion to vacate default judgment under section 473(d). (California Capital Ins. Co. v. Hoehn (2024) 17 Cal.5th 207, 226.) 

However, to obtain relief under section 473(d), Khalilian must show he was not properly served.  Plaintiff has filed a proof of service showing Khalilian was personally served by a sheriff’s deputy on October 20, 2023.  Khalilian cannot categorically deny that the deputy in fact handed him the summons and complaint.  He only says that he doesn’t recall receiving the documents because he was in the middle of preparing for a trial.  But that doesn’t establish that service was defective, and therefore, that Khalilian was denied due process.  The proof of service creates a rebuttable presumption, and Khalilian has not offered any facts to rebut that presumption.   

Instead, Khalilian asks for discovery that may help him rebut that presumption.  He requests “narrowly tailored” evidence regarding the sheriff’s complete service file, deputy notes, facility logs, visitor and law enforcement access records, and any document, property or legal mail records associated with the alleged service.  There is no basis for this discovery when Khalilian cannot dispute that he was served but only says he doesn’t recall that he was personally served.  It is the classic fishing expedition. 

Khalilian also maintains that he had no actual notice.  To the extent Khalilian seeks relief under section 473.5, his motion is untimely.  That provision requires that a motion be made within two years of the entry of default judgment, at the latest.  Khalilian filed his first motion to vacate default ( on August 10, 2026) more than two years after the entry of default judgment (on June 14, 2024). 

Next, Khalilian argues that the Court should grant him equitable relief based on an “extrinsic mistake.”  A trial court has inherent power to vacate a default judgment on equitable grounds. (Rappleyea v. Campbell (1994) 8 Cal.4th 975, 981; Aldrich v. San Fernando Valley Lumber Co. (1985) 170 Cal.App.3d 725, 736.)  

“One ground for equitable relief is extrinsic mistake—a term broadly applied when circumstances extrinsic to the litigation have unfairly cost a party a hearing on the merits.” (Rappleyea, 8 Cal.4th at 981; see Aldrich, 170 Cal.App.3d at  738.) “[E]xtrinsic mistake exists when the ground of relief is not so much the fraud or other misconduct of one of the parties as it is the excusable neglect of the defaulting party to appear and present his claim or defense. If that neglect results in an unjust judgment, without a fair adversary hearing, the basis for equitable relief on the ground of extrinsic mistake is present.” (Manson, Iver & York v. Black (2009) 176 Cal.App.4th 36, 47; see In re Marriage of Park (1980) 27 Cal.3d 337, 342.) 

To qualify for equitable relief based on extrinsic mistake, the defendant must demonstrate: (1) “a meritorious case”; (2) “a satisfactory excuse for not presenting a defense to the original action”; and (3) “diligence in seeking to set aside the default once the fraud [or mistake] had been discovered.” (In re Marriage of Stevenot (1984) 154 Cal.App.3d 1051, 1071.)  When “a default judgment has been obtained, equitable relief may be given only in exceptional circumstances.” (Rappleyea, 8 Cal.4th at 981.)  

Here, Khalilian has not shown he has a meritorious case.  To be sure, only a minimal showing is necessary. (Stiles v. Wallis (1983) 147 Cal.App.3d 1143, 1148.)  And the moving party does not have to guarantee success, or “demonstrate with certainty that a different result would obtain … . Rather, [it] must show facts indicating a sufficiently meritorious claim to entitle [it] to a fair adversary hearing.” (In re Marriage of Park, supra, 27 Cal.3d at 346.)  There are no such facts stated in Khalilian’s motion, only a reference to the “record” which he claims “presents unresolved issues”.  This bare assertion does not qualify as “facts,” even under a “minimal showing’ standard. 

Khalilian also asks that the Court correct the interest and damages amount.  He does not cite any authority that would allow the Court to do so.  Once the trial court has entered judgment, it is without power to correct or amend the judgment absent statutory authorization.  (APRI Ins. Co. SA v. Superior Court (1999) 76 Cal.App.4th 176, 182.)  Khalilian does not cite any statute that would allow the Court to amend the judgment under these circumstances.  Khalilian also does not indicate what the correct amount should be.  He asks the Court for “focused briefing and evidence on those issues before enforcing the disputed component.”  The Court declines Khalilian’s request for a correction of the judgment when Khalilian cites no supporting authority and does not even know what the error is in the judgment.   

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES Defendant’s motion to set aside the default/default judgment.   

 

DATED:  September 24, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 24SMCV01724    Hearing Date: September 24, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

SHARI ALEC GOLDBERG,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

THE LIDELL AT 10777 WILSHIRE HOA, et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 24SMCV01724 

  Hearing Date: September 24, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  DEFENDANT MICHAEL EASTER’s  

  MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT  

 

 

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This case arises from an assault at a parking garage in a condominium complex.  Plaintiff Shari Goldberg and Defendant Michael Easter reside at The Lidell, which is located in Los Angeles, California. (Defendant’s Statement of Facts (SOF) 4, 9.)  Defendant Sena Sumerlin was Easter’s girlfriend and/or fiance (SOF 6, 7).  She is now his wife.  Even before they got married, Sumerlin was a frequent guest at the Liddel.  Easter gave her a key to use while he was away, and the staff knew she stayed at the unit.  ((Additional Material Facts (“AMF”) 44.) 

On May 4, 2023, Sumerlin brutally attacked Plaintiff.  (AMF 111).  The attack resulted in severe injuries, requiring multiple brain surgeries that ultimately left her with significant mental deficits.    

Sumerlin attacked Plaintiff because of a prior confrontation that took place 15 minutes earlier on the same day.  Easter was not present in this prior encounter.  The conflict arose when Plaintiff was driving out of the garage at the Liddel when Sumerlin was driving in.  (AMF 60.)  Mr. Easter’s subsequent letter to the Liddel Homeowners Association (“HOA”) described the prior encounter as a dispute between Ms. Sumerlin and Plaintiff as to who had the right of way when Ms. Sumerlin was driving down the ramp while Plaintiff was turning to leave the garage about to go up the ramp.  (AMF 67.)   

Fifteen minutes after their first encounter, Plaintiff returned to the property and drove into the parking garage. (UMF 14; AMF 114.)  Sumerlin noticed the approaching car and pointed it out; Easter said he would go talk to Plaintiff. (AMF 93.) Easter asked her to stop, so Plaintiff stopped her car. (AMF 94.) Easter then told Plaintiff that she should slow down. (AMF 95.) Easter held Sumerlin back and moved her “about 10 or 12 feet from the car.” (AMF 96.) Easter restrained Sumerlin because he knew she was upset and didn’t want the situation to escalate. (AMF 97.)  

However, Sumerlin broke free from Easter, went to the driver’s window, and punched Plaintiff through the rolled-down window. (AMF 111.) The surveillance video, produced by the Liddel, shows the following: Sumerlin gestured toward Plaintiff’s car as it entered, Plaintiff stopped her car and Easter approached her and engaged in conversation, prolonging the encounter; Sumerlin then advanced, and Easter physically blocked her and pushed her away from the car; but Sumerlin broke free and punched Plaintiff through the open driver’s window. (AMF 108, 109, 110, 111; Exh. 15.)  

Easter claims that Sumerlin never verbalized to him or otherwise indicate that she had any intent to engage in a verbal or physical altercation with Plaintiff or anyone else.  He attests that he did not foresee the occurrence of the attack.  (SOF 17, 18.)  Sumerlin had never been convicted of a felony.  (SOF 24.) 

Easter also maintains that the Liddel documents incidents concerning threats to safety which occur between persons who are present at the Liddel.  And that prior to the occurrence of the attack on Plaintiff, there is no record of any incidents of violence by Sumerlin at the Liddel or any record that she threatened violence or was aggressive at the Liddel.  (SOF 26, 27.)  

Further, Easter claims that prior to the incident, he never witnessed Sumerlin engage in physical altercation with anyone.  (SOF 28.)  To his knowledge, prior to the attack on Plaintiff, Sumerlin had never been involved in any physical altercation with anyone at the Liddel or engaged in any confrontational or aggressive behavior toward others at the Liddel.  (SOF 29, 30.)    

Meanwhile, Plaintiff claims that Easter in fact knew that Sumerlin had been aggressive and threatened violence to an employee at the Liddel.  Weeks before the attack on Plaintiff, Sumerlin had threatened Nora Valladares who managed the valet department at The Liddel.  (AMF 48.)  Valladares had received a complaint about an unidentified vehicle on the property. She approached that vehicle in the visitors’ parking area early one morning and identified herself. (AMF 49, 50.) The woman inside, whom she later learned was Sumerlin, “became verbally violent and did not give me an opportunity to speak. I became afraid because she threatened too.” (AMF 51.) Sumerlin threatened Valladares with physical violence: “How about if you disappear before I break your face,” or “How about you disappear before I kick your ass.” (AMF 52.)  Easter then came down and apologized on Sumerlin’s behalf.  (AMF 55.)   

Easter states that he does not recall this incident or apologizing to Valladares.  (SOF 38.) He also says that while Valadares claims she reported this incident to the general manager, Narveil Fernandez, Fernandez says he has no memory of this report and no documents regarding the incident.  (SOF 39, 40.)   

Irrespective of Sumerlin’s activities at the Liddel, Plaintiff points out that Sumerlin was violent outside of the Liddel, and Easter knew about it.  In the year preceding the attack, Easter knew that Sumerlin’s ex-husband, Morris Halperin, had a domestic violence restraining order against her. (AMF 100.) He also knew in 2022 that any visitation between Sumerlin and her son had to be monitored by a professional monitor pursuant to court order. (AMF 101.) He knew, by late 2022, of a restraining order obtained by Sumerlin’s own former divorce attorney, Steven Weiss, and knew generally that there were other restraining order matters. (AMF 102.) He never asked her about the restraining orders; they “were not important to me.” (AMF 105.) He was aware that Sumerlin had been placed on a section 5150 involuntary psychiatric hold around 2018. (AMF 104.) He also knew of Sumerlin’s January 2023 arrest for driving under the influence, including a call from her from jail. (AMF 103.)  

On May 4, 2023, before Sumerlin assaulted Plaintiff, Easter knew “it was a high anxiety day” as she had received bad news that day and was scheduled to be cross-examined the next day in her divorce trial. (AMF 98.) And he knew the first confrontation that evening followed months of complaints by Sumerlin about Plaintiff’s driving: Sumerlin had complained to him that Plaintiff “drives too fast,” including a close call in the garage (“She almost hit me”). (AMF 99.) 

This hearing is on Easter’s motion for summary judgment.  Easter argues that he is entitled to summary judgment because he did not owe Plaintiff a duty to protect her against the conduct of a third party (Sumerlin) unless they were in a special relationship, which they were not.  Further, Easter argues that even if they were, the factors articulated by the court in Rowland v. Christian counsel against finding a duty of care in this case.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“[T]he party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of persuasion that there is no triable issue of material fact and that he is entitled to judgment as a matter of law[.] There is a triable issue of material fact if, and only if, the evidence would allow a reasonable trier of fact to find the underlying fact in favor of the party opposing the motion in accordance with the applicable standard of proof.”  (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 850.) “[T]he party moving for summary judgment bears an initial burden of production to make a prima facie showing of the nonexistence of any triable issue of material fact; if he carries his burden of production, he causes a shift, and the opposing party¿is then subjected to a burden of production of his own to make a prima facie showing of the existence of a triable issue of material fact.” (Id.) 

“On a summary judgment motion, the court must therefore consider what inferences favoring the opposing party a factfinder could reasonably draw from the evidence.¿While viewing the evidence in this manner, the court must bear in mind that its primary function is to identify issues rather than to determine issues. Only when the inferences are indisputable may the court decide the issues as a matter of law. If the evidence is in conflict, the factual issues must be resolved by trial.” (Binder v. Aetna Life Ins. Co. (1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 832, 839¿[cleaned up].)¿ 

Further, “the trial court may not weigh the evidence in the manner of a factfinder to determine whose version is more likely true. Nor may the trial court grant summary judgment based on the court's evaluation of credibility.” (Id. at 840¿[cleaned up]; see also¿Weiss v. People ex rel. Department of Transportation (2020) 9 Cal.5th 840, 864¿[“Courts deciding motions for summary judgment or summary adjudication may not weigh the evidence but must instead view it in the light most favorable to the opposing party and draw all reasonable inferences in favor of that party”].) 

EVIDENTIARY OBJECTIONS 

The Court overrules Plaintiff’s Objection Nos. 1-2, and sustains Plaintiff’s Objection Nos. 3-4.  The Court sustains Defendant’s objections to Plaintiff’s Exhibits 8, 9, 10, 11 and 13.   

DISCUSSION 

Easter argues that he did not owe a duty to Plaintiff to guard against the actions of Sumerlin, a third party, because he and Plaintiff were not in a special relationship.  In opposition, Plaintiff does not dispute that there is no special relationship here.  Instead, she argues that in cases of malfeasance, where a defendant makes a plaintiff’s position worse, there is no need to show a special relationship.  The Court agrees with Plaintiff.   

Each person has the general duty to exercise “reasonable care for the safety of others.” (Civ. Code, § 1714, subd. (a).)  This general duty to exercise reasonable care does not include a duty to control the conduct of third parties. (Zelig v. County of Los Angeles (2002) 27 Cal.4th 1112, 1129 [“[a]s a general rule, one owes no duty to control the conduct of another, nor to warn those endangered by such conduct”].) 

Despite the general rule of no duty with respect to third party conduct, courts have recognized exceptions where certain types of special relationships exist. (Doe v. L.A. County Dept. of Children & Family Services (2019) 37 Cal.App.5th 675, 682, 250 Cal. Rptr. 3d 62 ["A defendant does not owe a legal duty to protect against third party conduct, unless there exists a special relationship between the defendant and the plaintiff."].)  

However, the existence of a “special relationship” is not required where a plaintiff alleges a defendant committed malfeasance (or misfeasance), rather than merely nonfeasance. (Pedeferri v. Seidner Enterprises (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 359, 370; Lugtu v. California Highway Patrol (2001) 26 Cal.4th 703, 716-717.)  “Misfeasance exists when the defendant is responsible for making the plaintiff's position worse, i.e., defendant has created a risk. Conversely, nonfeasance is found when the defendant has failed to aid plaintiff through beneficial intervention.”  (Weirum v. RKO General, Inc. (1975) 15 Cal.3d 40, 49.)  

Here, Plaintiff argues that Easter made her position worse when he told Plaintiff to stop knowing of the prior conflict between Plaintiff and Sumerlin and that it was a “high anxiety day” for Sumerlin (who was upset about her divorce and potential complications with her pregnancy).  He then kept Plaintiff there, to discuss the prior conflict, and he expected Sumerlin would be violent because he restrained her and “didn’t want the situation to escalate”.   

Pamela L v. Farmer (1980) 112 Cal.App.3d 206 is analogous.  The case concerned the question of whether a wife was responsible for her husband’s molestation of three minor girls.  The defendant had invited and encouraged the girls to come to her house to swim, enticed them with refreshments, and assured the parents they would be safe, even though she knew that she would not be home, the children would be alone with her husband, and her husband had molested women and children in the past.  Under this set of facts, the court concluded that the defendant had increased the risk of harm to the plaintiff, and there was no requirement to show that the parties were in a special relationship.  (Id. at 210.)  

So it is here.  Easter flagged Plaintiff down, and kept her there, when he knew that Sumerlin who was nearby was upset and hostile towards Plaintiff.  He also knew about Sumerlin’s violent tendencies.  He has carefully crafted his statement of facts to suggest that he did not know of Sumerlin’s violent tendencies at the Liddel, but it doesn’t matter if she was violent at the Liddel or a block away.  What matters is that Easter knew she was violent prior to the incident.   

Easter knew that there were several restraining orders against Sumerlin, including one brought by her husband and another divorce attorney.  Easter also knew that Sumerlin had been accused of beating up a 75 year old man and putting him in the hospital.  Sumerlin was also accused of cruelty to her roommate’s pet cat.     

Of course, Easter testified that the restraining orders were dismissed and that no charges were brought against Sumerlin, but given the number of these accusations, a jury could reasonably discount Easter’s denials and conclude he was aware of Sumerlin’s violent tendencies.  Indeed, Easter physically restrained Sumerlin during the second encounter with Plaintiff, which a reasonable jury could conclude shows knowledge on his part of Sumerlin’s propensity for violence.   

Even assuming the relevant standard is Sumerlin’s violent tendencies at the Liddel, there is a triable issue as to whether Easter knew that Sumerlin had verbally threatened a Liddel employee with physical violence.  Valladares (who works at the Liddel) testified in deposition that Sumerlin threatened to “break her face” or “kick her ass,” and Easter later came down to apologize.  He told Valladreas: “I’m sorry. That wasn’t her [Sumerline’s] intention.” An apology suggests that Easter knew of Sumerlin’s threat of violence.   

Of course, Easter says he doesn’t recall making the apology, and that Valladares’ testimony was not unequivocal.  But these are matters for the jury to resolve. On a defendant’s motion for summary judgment, the Court must draw all reasonable inferences in the plaintiff’s favor.  (McCoy v. Pacific Maritime Assn. (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 283, 299 [“All reasonable inferences must be drawn in favor of the plaintiff [on a defendant’s motion for summary judgment] and conflicting evidence is to be disregarded.”].)   

Easter argues that the Court cannot consider Plaintiff’s malfeasance theory because it was not alleged in her Complaint.  The Court disagrees. 

The original Complaint did not name Easter or Sumerlin.  Plaintiff filed amendments to substitute Sumerlin for Doe 1 and Easter for Doe 2.  As to Doe Defendants, the original Complaint alleges that each Doe “is negligent, or in some other actionable manner, responsible for the events and happenings hereinafter referred to, and thereby negligently, or in some other actionable manner, legally and proximately caused the hereinafter described injuries and damages to PLAINTIFF GOLDBERG.”  These allegations are sufficient to encompass a theory of malfeasance. 

Even if there was no malfeasance, Plaintiff argues that the Court should still find that a duty exists because Easter voluntarily undertook a duty to come to her aid when he physically restrained Sumerlin.  However, Plaintiff has not established all the elements of the voluntary undertaking doctrine. 

Under that doctrine, “a volunteer who, having no initial duty to do so, undertakes to provide protective services to another, will be found to have a duty to exercise due care in the performance of that undertaking if one of two conditions is met: either (a) the volunteer's failure to exercise such care increases the risk of harm to the other person, or (b) the other person reasonably relies upon the volunteer’s undertaking and suffers injury as a result.” (Delgado, 36 Cal.4th at p. 249.)   

Here, Plaintiff has not made any showing as to what Easter did negligently when he was restraining Sumerlin.  The mere fact that Sumerlin was able to break free of Easter’s hold does not (by itself) show that Easter was negligent in the way he restrained Sumerlin.  Further, Plaintiff has proffered no evidence that she reasonably relied on Easter’s restraining of Sumerlin to remain at the scene.  She only makes that assertion in her opposition, without evidentiary support.  Accordingly, the Court concludes that the voluntary undertaking doctrine does not apply here. 

As the Court finds a duty based on malfeasance, it must next consider the policy factors articulated in Rowland v. Christian (1968) 69 Cal. 2d 108, 112-113.  There, the California Supreme Court set forth a “two-step inquiry”.  The first step assesses whether there is “a special relationship between the parties or some other set of circumstances giving rise to an affirmative duty to protect.” (Id.) If either exists, the court moves on to the second step and considers “whether relevant policy considerations counsel limiting that duty” (Id.) 

These considerations fall into two categories. The foreseeability factors evaluate “the foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff,” as well as related concerns such as “the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury” and “the closeness of the connection between the defendant’s conduct and the injury suffered.” (Id. at 113; accord, Kuciemba, 14 Cal.5th at 1021.) The public policy factors examine “the moral blame attached to the defendant’s conduct, the policy of preventing future harm, the extent of the burden to the defendant and consequences to the community of imposing a duty to exercise care with resulting liability for breach, and the availability, cost, and prevalence of insurance for the risk involved.” (Rowland, at 69 Cal.2d at 113; accord, Kuciemba, 14 Cal.5th at 1021–1022.) 

Different timeframes apply to the two sets of factors. (Kuciemba, supra, 14 Cal.5th at p. 1022.) The foreseeability factors “are assessed based on information available during the time of the alleged negligence,” whereas policy considerations—such as the burdens imposed on defendants—are forward-looking. (Id.) Both the foreseeability and the public policy factors are analyzed “‘at a relatively broad level of factual generality’” to determine not whether an exception is warranted in the specific circumstances of a particular case, but rather “‘whether carving out an entire category of cases from that general duty rule is justified by clear considerations of policy.’” (Id. at 1021.) In short, “‘the duty analysis is categorical, not case specific.’” (Id.) 

Here, the injury to a plaintiff was reasonably foreseeable where a defendant stops the plaintiff in front of another person with known violent tendencies who was already upset at the plaintiff for her alleged bad driving, and the defendant reopens an argument that was already a “trigger” for the aggressor.   

On the issue of burden, Easter could have avoided the incident by simply not flagging Plaintiff down and reopening the dispute.  The burden to him was minimal.  Easter argues that finding a duty in this case would create an enormous burden because “condominium owners would effectively be prevented from socializing with their significant others in their own home and prevented from inviting any vaguely bad-tempered friends/acquaintances to their home without incurring potential tort liability for a criminal act by their significant other/guest.”  However, finding a duty here does not prevent condominium owners from inviting ill-tempered friends to their homes.  Rather, the duty is not to put someone in the path of danger by flagging them down in front of a person with violent tendencies and to discuss a dispute that the defendant knew would upset the aggressor.     

The certainty of injury is not disputed here: Plaintiff suffered a traumatic brain injury with multiple surgeries. (Exh. 8, LIDDEL_000836; Exh. 3, Olimpio Depo. 67:14-23.) The connection between the conduct and injury is also clear.  Easter asked Plaintiff to stop; she stopped; the argument reopened, and Sumerlin then approached Plaintiff’s open window and struck her twice resulting in a severe brain injury.   

Moral blame also attaches to Easter who arguably knew about Sumerlin’s violent tendencies, knew of her disagreements with Plaintiff regarding Plaintiff’s driving, knew Sumerlin was already upset about other personal issues earlier in the day (involving her divorce and possible complications with her pregnancy), and yet he flagged Plaintiff down and put her in the path of danger.   

Easter cites to Romero v. Superior Court (2001) 89 Cal.App.4th 1068, 1083, which held that “an adult defendant who assumed a special relationship with a minor by inviting the minor into his or her home will be deemed to have owed a duty of care to take reasonable measures to protect the minor against an assault by another minor invitee while in the defendant’s home when the evidence and surrounding circumstances establish that the defendant had actual knowledge of, and thus must have known, the offending minor's assaultive propensities.”  (Id. at 1081.)  Here, there are issues of fact as to whether Easter had actual knowledge of Sumerlin’s “assaultive propensities” so Romero does not preclude the finding of a duty in this case. 

Easter’s other authorities are also distinguishable.  In Melton v. Boustred (2010) 183 Cal.App.4th 521, 527, homeowner defendant held a party at his residence with live music and alcohol. The party guests were strangers who responded to an open invitation on a social networking site.  (Id.) The plaintiffs were party guests who were physically attacked by unknown persons. (Id.) The court found there was no special relationship; i.e. no special between the plaintiffs and the homeowner defendant or between the homeowner defendant and the assailants. (Id. at 533, 536, 541.) 

In Eric J. v. Betty M. (1999) 76 Cal.App.4th 715, 723-724, 727, the guardian of a minor who was molested by his mother’s boyfriend, a convicted child molester, on premises owned by the boyfriend's family members, brought a premises liability and negligence action against the family members for failure to warn the minor’s mother of the boyfriend’s convictions.  As to the negligence cause of action, the court held that absent a special relationship, one cannot be held liable for mere nonfeasance, such as not protecting another from a criminal attack by a third party.  

Both cases involved nonfeasance.  In contrast, this case involves malfeasance.  This case is not rooted on Easter’s invitation to Sumerlin to have her stay at the Liddel.  Rather, it is based on the fact that Easter flagged Plaintiff down and put her in the direct path of danger, knowing of Sumerlin’s violent propensities.   

CONCLUSION 

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES Defendant Michael Easter’s motion for summary judgment.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.

Edward B. Moreton, Jr.

Defendants Mount Saint Mary’s University and Tavala Luciow move to continue the trial and related dates for a period of 90 days.  The motion is opposed by Plaintiffs and by Westside Cart Rentals and Evolution Electric Vehicles. 

The application is denied primarily because there is an insufficient showing of diligent preparation for trial by the moving parties and because there is an insufficient demonstration of inability by the moving parties’ counsel to continue to represent the moving parties at trial as scheduled, notwithstanding the unfortunate health problems and subsequent planned departure of one of their attorneys, Ms. Dooley.


Case Number: 24SMCV02855    Hearing Date: September 24, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

NOTABLE FINANCE, LLC,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

ROBERT ELLIS, et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  24SMCV02885 

  Hearing Date: September 24, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  plaintiff’s motion to VACATE  

  DISMISSAL AND ENTER JUDgment  

  pursuant to conditional  

  stipulated judgment  

  

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a breach of loan agreement case.  Plaintiff Notable Finance, LLC entered into a loan agreement with Defendant Robert Ellis in the amount of $60,000.  Under the terms of the agreement, Ellis agreed to repay the loan within 12 months.  Ellis defaulted.  Plaintiff sued for breach of contract and common counts, seeking $56,839 in damages. 

The parties settled on September 25, 2024.  Defendant agreed to pay Plaintiff $57,412, to be paid in installments, with the last payment due on August 20, 2027.  The parties stipulated that the Court would retain jurisdiction to enforce the agreement pursuant to section 664.6.  The parties also stipulated to a conditional dismissal of the complaint.  In the event of default, the settlement agreement provides the entire unpaid balance of $57,412 shall become due and payable less any payments received from Defendant.   

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s motion to vacate dismissal and to enter judgment in its favor pursuant to the parties’ settlement agreement.  According to Plaintiff, Defendant paid $14,400 with the last payment made on February 28, 2026.  Since February, Defendant has made no further payments as required under the settlement agreement.  Plaintiff asks for judgment to be entered in the amount of $56,839 plus court costs of $573 minus credits of $14,400 for a total of $43,012.00.  There was no oposition filed as of the posting of this tentative ruling.     

LEGAL STANDARD 

¿ 

Code Civ. Proc. §664.6 provides, in pertinent part, as follows: “If parties to pending litigation stipulate, in a writing signed by the parties outside the presence of the court or orally before the court, for settlement of the case, or part thereof, the court, upon motion, may enter judgment pursuant to the terms of the settlement.”¿¿ 

In hearing a Code Civ. Proc. §664.6 motion, the trial court may receive evidence, determine disputed facts, and enter terms of a settlement agreement as a judgment.¿ (Bowers v. Raymond J. Lucia Companies, Inc. (2012) 206 Cal.App.4th 724, 732.)  The Court may also receive oral testimony in addition to declarations. (Kohn v. Jaymar-Ruby, Inc. (1994) 23 Cal.App.4th 1530, 1533.)  The Court may interpret the terms and conditions of the settlement (Fiore v. Alvord (1985) 182 Cal.App.3d 561, 566), but the Court may not create material terms of a settlement, as opposed to deciding what terms the parties themselves have previously agreed upon.   (Weddington Productions, Inc. v. Flick (1998) 60 Cal.App.4th 793, 810).¿ 

Strict compliance with the statutory requirements is necessary before a court can enforce a settlement agreement under this statute.¿ (Sully-Miller Contracting Co. v. Gledson/Cashman Construction, Inc. (2002) 103 Cal.App.4th 30, 37.)¿ The party seeking to enforce a settlement “must first establish the agreement at issue was set forth ‘in a writing signed by the parties’ (§ 664.6) or was made orally before the court.¿ [Citation.]”¿ (Harris v. Rudin, Richman & Appel (1999) 74 Cal.App.4th 299, 304.)¿¿ 

The settlement must include the signatures of the parties seeking to enforce the agreement, and against whom enforcement is sought.¿ (J.B.B. Investment Partners, Ltd. v. Fair (2014) 232 Cal.App.4th 974, 985.)¿ “Parties” under Code Civ. Proc. § 664.6 means the litigants themselves, and not their attorneys, must expressly consent to settlement.¿ (Levy v. Superior Court (1995) 10 Cal.4th 578, 586 (“we conclude that the term ‘parties’ as used in section 664.6…means the litigants themselves, and does not include their attorneys of record”).)¿¿¿ 

DISCUSSION 

The Court’s November 13, 2024 order dismissed the case without prejudice.  The order states that the Court “shall retain jurisdiction under California Code of Civil Procedure section 664.6. to set aside said dismissal, and enter a Judgment upon showing of default of the terms of the Stipulation.”  

Plaintiff’s counsel has submitted a declaration attesting that Defendant has defaulted on the settlement agreement.  As the settlement checks were to be made to counsel, she has personal knowledge about the default. 

Plaintiff has also submitted the settlement agreement, which is authenticated by counsel.  The settlement agreement shows it was signed by both parties.  (Ex. 1 to D’Anna Decl.)  Defendant does not argue that the settlement is not valid and enforceable.   

Under the settlement agreement, once Defendant defaults, the entire sum of $57,412 is due and payable, less any amounts paid by Defendant.  However, Plaintiff only seeks the pre-judgment amount of $56,839, and not the settlement sum, less a credit of $14,400 reflecting payments made by Defendant before his default.   

Plaintiff also seeks court costs of $573.  Under paragraph 7 of the settlement agreement, the parties agreed to bear their.own attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with the Action except in the event of a default of the settlement agreement.  Accordingly, Plaintiff is entitled to seek costs pursuant to paragraph 7.   

The Court concludes that there is a valid settlement agreement; Defendant defaulted on the settlement agreement, and pursuant to the terms of the settlement agreement, Plaintiff is entitled to immediate payment as well as costs.    

CONCLUSION 

Based on the foregoing, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion to vacate dismissal and to enter judgment in the amount of $43,012 in Plaintiff’s favor and against Defendant.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED: September 24, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 26SMCV02777    Hearing Date: September 24, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

LIDA DANIELYAN,   

  

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

CEDARS-SINAI MEDICAL CENTER, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 26SMCV02777 

  Hearing Date:  September 24, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  DEFENDANT’S DEMURRER TO  

  COMPLAINT  

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a medical malpractice case.  On October 27, 2025, Plaintiff was admitted to Defendant Cedars-Sinai Medical Center for a hip replacement surgery.  Plaintiff claims she was discharged despite her reporting to Cedars staff that she was dizzy and weak and while she was still under the effects of anesthesia.  Plaintiff claims there were no clinical reassessments done prior to proceeding with the discharge.  

A Cedars-Sinai employee transported Plaintiff by wheelchair to the parking structure.  As the employee attempted to transfer Plaintiff from the wheelchair into the waiting vehicle, he released his hold on Plaintiff to adjust something in the car. He did so without warning Plaintiff and without taking any steps to ensure that Plaintiff was secured or otherwise capable of supporting herself.   

At that moment, Plaintiff, who remained under the heavy effects of anesthesia and had already reported feeling dizzy and weak, fell to the ground, landing on her back on the surface of the parking lot.  As a result of the fall, Plaintiff dislocated and fractured the very hip that had been surgically replaced only hours earlier.  

Cedars-Sinai personnel responded to the scene and, after being unable to assist Plaintiff to a seated position, used a Hoyer lift to transfer her onto a gurney. Plaintiff was then taken to the emergency room, where radiographic imaging confirmed the hip fracture.  

The very next day, Plaintiff underwent a second surgical procedure to repair the injuries caused by the fall. Following the second surgery, Plaintiff remained hospitalized for approximately five additional days. 

This action ensued.  Plaintiff sues Cedars for (1) professional negligence, (2) general negligence, (3) negligent hiring/training/supervision/retention, and (4) negligent infliction of emotional distress.   

This hearing is on Cedars’ demurrer to the Complaint, specifically the second cause of action for general negligence.  Cedars argues that the negligence claim is one for professional negligence because it involves the rendering of medical services, and as such, it is duplicative of the first cause of action.  Cedars also represents that Plaintiff has stipulated to the dismissal of the fourth cause of action for negligent infliction of emotional distress. 

MEET AND CONFER 

Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41 requires that before the filing of a demurrer the moving party “shall meet and confer in person or by telephone” with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to demurrer for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a).)  The parties are to meet and confer at least five days before the date the responsive pleading is due. (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a)(2).)  Thereafter, the moving party shall file and serve a declaration detailing their meet and confer efforts. (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a)(3).)  Defendant submits the Declaration of Saa K. Mores who attests that the parties met and conferred by email and telephone.  The parties were able to resolve their disputes as to the negligent infliction and emotional distress claim but were not able to agree as to the general negligence claim.  This satisfies Defendant’s meet and confer obligations.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“[A] demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the allegations in a complaint.” (Lewis v. Safeway, Inc. (2015) 235 Cal.App.4th 385, 388.)  A demurrer can be used only to challenge defects that appear on the face of the pleading under attack or from matters outside the pleading that are judicially noticeable.  (See Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994 (in ruling on a demurrer, a court may not consider declarations, matters not subject to judicial notice, or documents not accepted for the truth of their contents).)  For purposes of ruling on a demurrer, all facts pleaded in a complaint are assumed to be true, but the reviewing court does not assume the truth of conclusions of law. (Aubry v. Tri-City Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  

Leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (See Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 349 (court shall not “sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is any reasonable possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment”); Kong v. City of Hawaiian Gardens Redevelopment Agency (2002) 108 Cal.App.4th 1028, 1037 (“A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally construed, can state a cause of action under any theory or if there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured by amendment.”). The burden is on the complainant to show the Court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.)  

DISCUSSION 

Uncertainty 

Cedars argues that the Complaint is “fatally uncertain as pled” (Demurrer at 2) but it never explains how that is so.  Demurrers for uncertainty under Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10, subdivision (e) are disfavored. (Lickiss v. Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (2012) 208 Cal.App.4th 1125, 1135.) “A demurrer for uncertainty is strictly construed, even where a complaint is in some respects uncertain, because ambiguities can be clarified under modern discovery procedures.” (Khoury v. Maly's of California, Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 616.)   

A demurrer for uncertainty will be sustained only where the complaint is so bad that the defendant cannot reasonably respond. (Id.)  Here, the FAC is not so bad that Cedars cannot properly respond to it.  Cedars’ demurrer makes clear that Cedars knows the underlying facts and theories of Plaintiff’s claims.  The allegations are simple -- Plaintiff fell while being transported out of the hospital, and Plaintiff is suing for professional and general negligence.   

General Negligence 

Cedars argues that Plaintiff’s general negligence claim is duplicative of the professional negligence claim because the transport of Plaintiff into the van/car constitutes the provision of medical services, and therefore, the general negligence claim is merely a restatement of the professional negligence claim.  Cedars next argues that the transport of a patient to a car after the patient has had surgery constitutes professional negligence, not general negligence.  The Court agrees. 

The determination of whether a claim is one for professional negligence or ordinary negligence is significant because a professional negligence claim is harder to bring than an ordinary negligence claim.  A professional negligence claim has a shorter statute of limitations.  It requires a 90-day notice period where a plaintiff must inform the provider of his/her intent to sue.  And a plaintiff must obtain a certificate of merit from a medical expert confirming the claim’s validity.   It also imposes a $250,000 cap on non-economic damages, and a plaintiff must obtain leave of court before seeking punitive damages.   

In a medical negligence claim, “professional negligence” has four elements: (1) “a negligent act or omission to act by a health care provider in the rendering of professional services,” (2) “which act or omission is the proximate cause of a personal injury or wrongful death,” (3) “provided that such services are within the scope of services for which the provider is licensed,” and (4) “which are not within any restriction imposed by the licensing agency or licensed hospital.” (Flores v. Presbyterian Intercommunity Hosp. (2016) 63 Cal.4th 75, 84, quoting Code Civ. Proc. § 340.5(2).)  

Here, there is no dispute that Cedars is a healthcare provider, and that the Cedars is licensed to care for patients such as Plaintiff.  There is also no dispute that the transporter was acting in the course and scope of his employment with Cedars.  The issue is whether the act of transporting a patient into a car at a hospital parking garage constitutes the provision of professional services.   

To be sure, pushing a wheelchair does not require special skill or medical knowledge.  But “professional services” does not apply only to those specific tasks that require advanced medical skills and training.  A medical professional or other hospital staff member may commit a negligent act in rendering medical care, thereby causing a patient's injury, even where no particular medical skills were required to complete the task at hand. (Flores v. Presbyterian Intercommunity Hosp. (2016) 63 Cal.4th 75, 89.) 

For example, a hospital’s negligent failure to prevent a patient from becoming separated from an oxygen ventilator occurs in the “rendering of professional services” (§ 340.5, subd. (2)), “regardless of whether separation was caused by the ill-considered decision of a physician or the accidental bump of a janitor's broom” (Taylor v. U.S. (9th Cir. 1987) 821 F.2d 1428, 1432).  

If a doctor has determined that a hospitalized patient’s medical needs require a special diet, and the patient is injured because a hospital employee negligently gives the patient the wrong food, the hospital has inflicted injury in the rendering of professional services to the patient.  (Flores, 63 Cal.4th at 89.) 

If hospital staff places a violently coughing patient on a gurney for X-rays, and the patient falls to the ground after the staff negligently leaves her unsecured while the film is being developed, the hospital has caused injury in the rendering of professional services to the patient, even though fastening straps requires no special skill. (See Bellamy, 50 Cal.App.4th 797.) 

And if a patient fell because a hospital staff employee neglected to put up the bed rails (which is a task anyone can perform), the act is still a professional service.  (Flores, 63 Cal.4th at 89; Murillo v. Good Samaritan Hospital (1979) 99 Cal. App. 3d 50, 52-54.)   The decision whether or not to raise the bedrails on the plaintiff's bed came within the defendant hospital’s “duty 'to use reasonable care and diligence in safeguarding a patient committed to its charge.” ( Id. at 55.)  “Whether it was negligent to leave the bedrails down during the night while plaintiff was asleep is a question involving hospital’s duties to recognize the condition of patients under its care and to take appropriate measures for their safety.” (Id. at 56.) 

So it is here.  The transport of Plaintiff was part of her medical care, to ensure she safely got into her car after the surgical procedure.  Accordingly, Plaintiff’s general negligence claim is truly a professional negligence claim.   

Plaintiff’s reliance on Gutierrez v. Tostado (2025) 18 Cal.5th 222 is misplaced.  There, the plaintiff in Gutierrez was not a patient.  The plaintiff was driving his car when he was rear-ended by an ambulance transporting a patient.  The defendants in Gutierrez argued that because the injury occurred in the rendering of professional services to a patient, MICRA applied.  The California Supreme Court disagreed, holding that MICRA does not apply to a plaintiff who is part of the public at large and is unrelated to the patient to whom the professional services are being rendered.  The Guiterrez court distinguished the case before it to a hypothetical where a janitor’s broom accidentally falls and disconnects a patient’s ventilator.  The Guiterrez court noted that the janitor example would be a case of professional negligence.  (Id. at 232-233.) 

Cedars next argues that because Plaintiff’s general negligence claim is really a professional negligence claim, the claims are duplicative, and the general negligence claim should be dismissed.   

There is a split authority on whether a demurrer can be sustained on the ground that a cause of action is duplicative.  Some courts have recognized it as a proper basis for sustaining a demurrer. (See Palm Springs Villas II Homeowners Assn., Inc. v. Parth (2016) 248 Cal.App.4th 268, 290 [“Regardless, as Parth argues, the cause of action for breach of governing documents appears to be duplicative of the cause of action for breach of fiduciary duty. This court has recognized this as a basis for sustaining a demurrer.”]); see also Award Metals, Inc. v. Superior Court (1991) 228 Cal.App.3d 1128, 1135 ["But stating them in two causes of action, as real party has done, is merely duplicative pleading which adds nothing to the complaint by way of fact or theory. For that reason, the demurrer should have been sustained as to this cause of action . . . ."].) 

Other courts have found that a cause of action is not subject to demurrer merely for being duplicative of another cause of action. (See Blickman Turkus, LP v. MF Downtown Sunnyvale, LLC (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 858, 889-90 [“BTC went on to argue that this was a distinction without legal significance, and that the court should sustain the demurrer because the third cause of action 'mirrors [the] first cause of action for concealment and is duplicative.’ This is not a ground on which a demurrer may be sustained.”].)   

The Blickman court first noted that the language of C.C.P. §430.10 does not authorize a demurrer on grounds of redundancy.  (Blickman, 162 Cal.App.4th at 890.) The Blickman court observed that the practice of sustaining a demurrer to a duplicative cause of action was actually grounded in language no longer present in the statutory scheme. (Id.) Although the statute authorizing a motion to strike, Code Civ. Proc. §436(a), did previously authorize courts to strike out "irrelevant and redundant" matter, that language has since been removed. (Id.) The court observed that the modern statute contained no analogous language authorizing the striking of redundant material. (Id.) 

The Court finds the reasoning in Blickman persuasive.  Section 430.30 identifies eight bases for a demurrer, and redundancy is not one of them.  (See Auto Equity Sales, Inc. v. Superior Court of Santa Clara County (1962) 57 Cal.2d 450, 456, (Where appellate decisions are in conflict, the court exercising inferior jurisdiction can and must make a choice between the conflicting decisions) 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

Based on the foregoing, the Court OVERRULES the demurrer to the general negligence claim and SUSTAINS the demurrer to the negligent infliction of emotional distress claim. 

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.
